title: Only Happens Here: 10 Traditions That Make No Sense Anywhere Else
description: Ten documented Georgia Tech rituals, events, objects, and recurring practices, from a fictional alumnus to Homecoming races on tricycles and foot.

cards.title: Follow a 1930 Ford Onto the Field
cards.subtitle: The Ramblin’ Reck leads every Georgia Tech home-football entrance
cards.notes: Watch before kickoff as the gold-and-white Model A leads the team into Bobby Dodd Stadium, a duty it has performed since 1961.
cards.short_summary: Georgia Tech begins each home football game behind its mechanical mascot.
cards.evidence_claim: Georgia Tech documents that its 1930 Ford Model A Sport Coupe has led the football team onto the field at every home game since September 30, 1961.
cards.source_title: Georgia Tech Traditions: The Ramblin’ Reck
cards.access_notes: Visible to ticketed spectators at home football games; confirm the current athletics schedule and stadium rules before attending.

cards.title: Let the Whistle Dismiss Class
cards.subtitle: A steam blast still structures the academic day
cards.notes: Listen near the power plant around class changes; the whistle also marks touchdowns, home victories, and remembrance ceremonies.
cards.short_summary: An industrial-era steam signal remains part of Georgia Tech’s daily soundscape.
cards.evidence_claim: Georgia Tech identifies the steam whistle as its oldest recorded tradition and says it signals class changes, touchdowns, home football victories, and the When the Whistle Blows memorial ceremony.
cards.access_notes: The whistle can be heard outdoors on campus; its weekday pattern follows the class schedule and may change with Institute operations.

cards.title: Write a Semester Onto a Gold Cap
cards.subtitle: First-year students personalize a Convocation keepsake
cards.notes: If you receive a RAT cap, add your name, major, hometown, graduation year, and game scores using the documented layout.
cards.short_summary: A marked-up gold cap becomes a compact record of a student’s first year.
cards.evidence_claim: Georgia Tech says first-year students receive RAT caps at Convocation and documents how students traditionally add personal information and football scores to them.
cards.access_notes: Cap distribution is associated with first-year Convocation; participation in decorating or wearing one is voluntary.

cards.title: Collect the Traditions Handbook
cards.subtitle: A revived campus guide is distributed to entering students
cards.notes: Pick up the T-Book through first-year programming, then use its sections on Tech history, songs, spirit, and RAT caps as a reference.
cards.short_summary: Georgia Tech’s century-old student handbook connects each entering class with campus customs.
cards.evidence_claim: Georgia Tech documents that the T-Book originated as a new-student guide, was revived in print in 2008, and is distributed to entering students at Convocation and through first-year programs.
cards.access_notes: Physical copies are intended for entering students and distributed through Convocation and selected first-year programs; availability may vary.

cards.title: Race Tricycles Around a Parking Deck
cards.subtitle: Homecoming teams combine pedaling, pit work, and engineering
cards.notes: Watch teams attempt eight laps around Peters Parking Deck while completing required front-wheel rotations with their pit crews.
cards.short_summary: Georgia Tech turns children’s tricycles into a technical Homecoming team challenge.
cards.evidence_claim: Georgia Tech documents the Mini 500 as a Ramblin’ Reck Club tradition held since 1969, with teams racing tricycles for eight laps around Peters Parking Deck and rotating the front wheel three times.
cards.access_notes: This is a scheduled Homecoming event; team participation has rules and advance organization, while spectator arrangements vary by year.

cards.title: Run Up Freshman Hill for Cake
cards.subtitle: A pre-sunrise first-year race ends with cupcakes
cards.notes: Eligible first-year students can register for the half-mile Homecoming run; spectators should confirm that year’s early start and route.
cards.short_summary: A former cross-country tryout survives as a short first-year Homecoming race with baked rewards.
cards.evidence_claim: Georgia Tech says the Cake Race began in 1911 and now takes place before sunrise on Homecoming morning as a half-mile first-year race ending atop Freshman Hill, with cupcakes for finishers and cakes for winners.
cards.source_title: Georgia Tech Traditions: Freshmen Cake Race
cards.access_notes: Participation is intended for first-year students and requires current event instructions; the route and start time should be reconfirmed each Homecoming.

cards.title: Parade Human-Powered Contraptions
cards.subtitle: Student-built machines join classic cars at Homecoming
cards.notes: Stand along the announced Homecoming route to see classic cars, fixed bodies, and human-powered contraptions led by the Reck.
cards.short_summary: An unsafe road race evolved into a campus parade centered on inventive vehicles.
cards.evidence_claim: Georgia Tech says students created the Ramblin’ Wreck Parade after the 1929–30 Old Ford Race was deemed unsafe; today its categories include classic cars, fixed bodies, and human-powered contraptions.
cards.source_title: Georgia Tech Traditions: Ramblin’ Wreck Parade
cards.access_notes: Attend only on the published Homecoming route and remain in designated spectator areas; timing and street controls vary annually.

cards.title: Meet the Alumnus Who Never Existed
cards.subtitle: A 1927 enrollment prank became a durable campus persona
cards.notes: Trace Burdell’s fictional biography through Tech history, but leave modern registrations and official records untouched.
cards.short_summary: Generations of Yellow Jackets have extended the biography of an imaginary graduate.
cards.evidence_claim: Georgia Tech documents that student William Edgar Smith created George P. Burdell with a spare enrollment form in 1927 and that later students continued placing the fictional alumnus into campus and public records.
cards.source_title: Georgia Tech Traditions: George P. Burdell
cards.access_notes: Explore the documented story without submitting false registrations, altering systems, or placing the fictional name in official records.

cards.title: Learn Tech Traditions in One Night
cards.subtitle: A welcome-week festival and show introduce campus customs
cards.notes: Check the Week of Welcome calendar for T-Night, then use its booths and stage program to learn traditions and meet student groups.
cards.short_summary: Georgia Tech packages its customs and student organizations into a first-week festival and show.
cards.evidence_claim: Georgia Tech’s 2025 calendar documented T-Night as a free, all-student Traditions Night featuring tradition booths, student-organization showcases, a festival, and an indoor show.
cards.access_notes: The cited event occurred in 2025; consult the current Week of Welcome calendar before relying on its date, venue, format, or admission details.

cards.entity_name: Up With the White and Gold
cards.title: Answer Red and Black With White and Gold
cards.subtitle: One of Georgia Tech’s two documented fight songs
cards.notes: Learn the short fight song from Tech’s traditions page, then listen for the marching band’s arrangement at campus ceremonies and games.
cards.short_summary: A 1919 song turns Georgia Tech’s colors and rivalry into a compact musical ritual.
cards.evidence_claim: Georgia Tech identifies “Up With the White and Gold,” written by Frank Roman and released in 1919, as one of the Institute’s two fight songs honoring its old-gold-and-white colors.
cards.access_notes: The song may be heard at ceremonies and athletics events; event admission requirements depend on the specific performance venue.

warnings: T-Night is supported by a direct 2025 event page; its recurrence, date, format, and free admission must be reconfirmed for later years.
Event routes, eligibility rules, registration procedures, and spectator access can change; consult current Georgia Tech schedules before attending.
